content.title: Official Blind Review #1
content.review_assessment:_thoroughness_in_paper: I read the paper at least twice and used my best judgement in assessing the paper.
content.review:
This paper introduces LSSGD [1] in the privacy-preserving empirical risk minimization to improve the utility upper bound under the same privacy budget. The experiments show that the proposed method called DP-LSSGD outperforms the baseline method--DP-SGD [2].

My major concerns are as follows.
1. The improvement of the utility upper bound is insignificant. Table 1 shows that the utility upper bounds of DP-LSSGD and DP-SGD have the same order.
2. The novelty is incremental. The key method in this paper--LSSGD--was proposed in [1].
3. Table 2 in [3] shows that DP-SVRG [3] outperforms the baseline method--DP-SGD. The authors may want to conduct more experiments to compare DP-LSSGD with other related work including DP-SVRG.
4. The authors may want to provide the problem setup of the privacy-preserving empirical risk minimization in detail.


[1] S. Osher, B. Wang, P. Yin, X. Luo, M. Pham, and A. Lin. Laplacian Smoothing Gradient Descent. ArXiv:1806.06317, 2018.
[2] R. Bassily, A. Smith, and A. Thakurta. Private Empirical Risk Minimization: Efficient Algorithms and Tight Error Bounds. In 55th Annual IEEE Symposium on Foundations of Computer Science (FOCS 2014) , 2014.
[3] D. Wang, M. Ye, and J. Xu. Differentially Private Empirical Risk Minimization Revisited: Faster and More General. In Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems (NIPS 2017), 2017.

content.title: Reply to Review #1
content.comment:
Thank you for your valuable feedback and thoughtful reviews. Below we address your concerns about our work.

Q1. The improvement of the utility upper bound is insignificant. Table 1 shows that the utility upper bounds of DP-LSSGD and DP-SGD have the same order.

Answer: Our utility bound for the convex optimization problem trades off the initialization  (i.e., $D_\sigma$) and the Gaussian noise injection, and our numerical results show that the later one is the dominating term. Although the improvement of the utility bound is at a constant level, this constant is much less than one, especially for high dimensional problems. More importantly, we show by experiments that the DP-LSSGD can significantly improve the utility of both convex and nonconvex machine learning models. For instance, within our testing regime, compared with the TensorFlow differential privacy benchmark, DP-LSSGD can improve the accuracy of the differentially private logistic regression, neural nets for MNIST classification by up to 3.78% and 5.0%, respectively. Also, due to the circulant structure of the Laplacian smoothing matrix, we can use fast Fourier transform to compute the Laplacian smoothing with negligible overhead in memory and computational time.


Q2. The novelty is incremental. The key method in this paper--LSSGD--was proposed in [1].

Answer: While LSSGD was proposed in [1], the authors focus on studying variance reduction for SGD with applications in training deep neural nets. To the best of our knowledge, we are the first one that leveraged the denoising property of the Laplacian matrix to improve the utility for privacy preserving machine learning. The proposed DP-LSSGD can remarkably improve the utility of the trained differentially private machine learning models in practice. We believe that the use of Laplacian smoothing in privacy preserving machine learning has never been studied before and is novel.



Q3. Table 2 in [3] shows that DP-SVRG [3] outperforms the baseline method--DP-SGD. The authors may want to conduct more experiments to compare DP-LSSGD with other related work including DP-SVRG.

Answer: As suggested by the reviewer, we have conducted experiments to compare DP-LSSGD with DP-SVRG. 
First, we have the following eps vs. accuracy results for differentially private logistic regression on the MNIST dataset:
———————————————————————————————--
eps, delta=10^-5                   0.30             0.25                 0.20
———————————————————————————————--
DP-LSSGD(sigma=3)        85.11 (0.45)   82.97 (0.48)  82.22 (0.28)
DP-SGD                            81.74 (0.96)   81.45 (1.59)  78.92 (1.14)
DP-SVRG                          84.31 (0.31)   82.35 (0.36)  79.92 (0.29)
———————————————————————————————-
We can see that DP-SVRG outperforms DP-SGD in training the logistic regression model. However, DP-SVRG is slightly worse than DP-LSSGD. We think this is because DP-SVRG did not remove the injected Gaussian noise, and we believe that integrating DP-SVRG with Laplacian smoothing can further improve the performance for training convex ML models.

Second, we have the following eps vs. accuracy results for CNN on the MNIST dataset:
———————————————————————————————-
eps, delta=10^-5                 7.0          5.0       3.0     1.0     0.8       0.6
———————————————————————————————-
DP-LSSGD                      97.19     96.77   96.68   95.28    94.57   93.56
DP-LSAdam                     97.18    96.45    96.36   95.09   94.06    92.72
DP-SGD                           96.83    96.55    96.49   95.01   94.32    93.18
DP-Adam                         96.91     96.26    96.05   94.88   93.91   93.23
DP-SVRG                        96.88     96.31    95.69   94.99   94.50   93.14
———————————————————————————————-
For the high privacy regime (small epsilon), DP-SVRG outperforms DP-SGD and DP-Adam, on par with DP-LSSGD and DP-LSAdam; for low privacy regime (large epsilon), DP-SVRG is worse than DP-LSSGD and DP-LSAdam.

For all the above results, we have performed an exhaustive tuning for all the hyperparameters of the different DP optimization algorithms.

In the revised manuscript, we have included more related references.


Q4. The authors may want to provide the problem setup of the privacy-preserving empirical risk minimization in detail.

Answer: As suggested by the reviewer, we have provided a detailed problem setup of empirical risk minimization at the beginning of Section 2., and DP ERM at the beginning of Section 2.2 in the revised manuscript.

==========================================================
We hope we have answered all your questions about our work, and we would appreciate more constructive feedback from you.

content.title: Official Blind Review #3
content.review_assessment:_checking_correctness_: I assessed the sensibility of the derivations and theory.
content.review:
This paper proposes an algorithm called DP-LSSGD, which can improve upon DPSGD in terms of utility with Laplacian smoothing. The authors provide convergence guarantee and experimental evaluations demonstrating the advantage of the proposed algorithm over DPSGD and DPAdam.

The proposed method seems like a good method to have for improving the gradient-based DP learning algorithms. I have some more comments/questions:
1. It seems to me that the experiments mainly considers high privacy (epsilon < 1) regime. This might be a bit too strict in practice. Given that Figure 5 seems to suggest that the advantage of the proposed method is less significant in the higher epsilon regime (though still pretty low to me), I think the authors might consider comment more on this matter. Maybe adding a plot showing final accuracy vs. epsilon (for epsilon going all the way up to 5 or 10) can also help.
2. You mentioned that the accuracy of DPSGD decreases after some epoch. Can this possibly be fixed by a brief hyperparameter selection? I feel like experiments from related work don’t usually have such a problem. Maybe it would look fairer if the best parameter is used for everyone. Besides, since DPSGD seems to work better in the beginning, would you consider using DPSGD first and then change to DPLSSGD or increasing sigma gradually?
3. I’m not very familiar with the field but I guess there might be other existing denoising methods for SGD or other gradient descent method. If so, why did you pick the LSSGD algorithm and do you think other denoising methods can be equally helpful for DP training?

content.title: Reply to review #3
content.comment:
Thank you for your valuable feedback and thoughtful reviews. Below we address your concerns about our work.

Q1. It seems to me that the experiments mainly considers high privacy (epsilon < 1) regime. This might be a bit too strict in practice. Given that Figure 5 seems to suggest that the advantage of the proposed method is less significant in the higher epsilon regime (though still pretty low to me), I think the authors might consider comment more on this matter. Maybe adding a plot showing final accuracy vs. epsilon (for epsilon going all the way up to 5 or 10) can also help.

Answer: As suggested, we have also conducted experiments on a low privacy regime. Below is a comparison between different optimization algorithms on training CNN for MNIST classification:
—————————————————————————
$\epsilon, \delta=10^-5$      7.0          5.0       3.0     1.0   
—————————————————————————
DP-LSSGD                      97.19     96.77   96.68   95.28   
DP-LSAdam                     97.18    96.45    96.36   95.09   
DP-SGD                           96.83    96.55    96.49   95.01   
DP-Adam                         96.91     96.26    96.05   94.88  
—————————————————————————-
We see that even in the low privacy regime (large $\epsilon$), Laplacian smoothing can also improve the utility of the trained model. In practice, the high privacy regime is usually more important and challenging. Privacy-preserving machine learning with a low privacy guarantee is much less challenging than the high privacy scenario. In the revised manuscript, we have also plotted the results in the above table.


Q2. You mentioned that the accuracy of DPSGD decreases after some epoch. Can this possibly be fixed by a brief hyperparameter selection? I feel like experiments from related work don’t usually have such a problem. Maybe it would look fairer if the best parameter is used for everyone. Besides, since DPSGD seems to work better in the beginning, would you consider using DPSGD first and then change to DPLSSGD or increasing sigma gradually?

Answer: We have tried different sets of hyperparameters, the reason for the accuracy of DPSGD decays after some epoch is because we inject a very big noise in the stochastic gradient to guarantee strong differential privacy.

   Yes, it is a very good idea to consider adaptive sigma, and it is under our consideration. We are also working on finding the optimal scheduling of the sigma for Laplacian smoothing. So far, for adaptive sigma, we do not have any theoretical guarantee about the utility of the final models. 


Q3. I’m not very familiar with the field but I guess there might be other existing denoising methods for SGD or other gradient descent method. If so, why did you pick the LSSGD algorithm and do you think other denoising methods can be equally helpful for DP training?

Answer: Yes, we agree there might be other denoising methods to improve the utility of the trained differentially private models. The denoising methods should guarantee convergence of noise injected SGD in a certain sense and should not slow down the training process too much. Laplacian smoothing matrix is a positive definite matrix with small condition number 1+4sigma (independent of the dimension of the underlying problem), and it will not hurt the convergence rate. Also, post-processing by the Laplacian smoothing matrix can reduce the noise in the noisy stochastic gradient. Moreover, we can compute the Laplacian smoothing very efficiently by the fast Fourier transform.

=================================
We hope we have answered all your questions about our work, and we would appreciate more constructive feedback from you.

content.title: Official Blind Review #2
content.review_assessment:_checking_correctness_: I assessed the sensibility of the derivations and theory.
content.review:
Differentially private (DP) algorithms give provable privacy guarantees at the cost of a non-negligible loss in terms of utility. Motivated by such empirical observations, this paper proposes to lift the utility of the DP-SGD algorithm that is used to train differentially private DNNs by a mechanism called Laplacian smoothing. The authors claim that under the same privacy budget, the proposed methods enjoys better utility guarantees, measured in terms of optimality gap (convex cases) and stationary gap (norm of the gradient, nonconvex cases). 

Overall, the paper is well-written and easy to follow. However, I am not very convinced by the claim that the proposed DP-LSSGD algorithm enjoys better utility guarantees under the same privacy budget. Specifically, if we check the results in both convex and nonconvex cases in Table 1, it turns out the convergence rates (optimality/stationary gap) in terms of d, n and \epsilon are exactly the same between the classic DP-SGD and the proposed DP-LSSGD. The only difference lies in the constants, which are fixed and do not matter too much. If we check the results more carefully, it is even not clear in the convex case the constant $\gamma\cdot D_\sigma$ is smaller than $D_0$. From this perspective it is not clear to me what's the essential improvement here? 

The main idea of the Laplacian smoothing is to precondition the original gradient descent by a fixed matrix $A_\sigma$. The authors claim that the LS method could help to avoid spurious minima and reduce the variance of SGD. I am not sure about this point, since in the literature there are many data-dependent preconditioning methods, including AdaGrad, Adam, AdaReg, etc., but none of them is free of the local-minima problem. So it's not clear to me why a fixed preconditioning matrix will help here? The final DP-LSSGD algorithm is a combination of the original DPSGD algorithm with a preconditioning matrix given by $A_\sigma$, similar to what is done in LSSGD. 

The main contribution of this manuscript lies in Section 3, i.e., the theoretical analysis of the convergence rate of the proposed algorithm in both convex and nonconvex settings. The results (in terms of convergence rate) are the same as the ones in the non-private settings. Just a comment, with further assumptions, e.g., strong convexity in the convex case, the authors could potentially improve the $O(1/\epsilon)$ rate to linear convergence of $O(\log(1/\epsilon))$. So the main take-home message here is that privacy does not sacrifice convergence speed, which is already known in the literature. 

Experiments comparing DP-LSSGD versus other DP variants are conducted. In Figure 5, it is shown that DP-LSSGD is indeed better than DP-SGD in terms of accuracy, but is slightly worse than DP-Adam. A combination of the Laplacian smoothing with DP-Adam gives the best result in terms of accuracy in most of the cases, which is a plus.

Overall, I think there is indeed some novel contribution in this paper, but I feel it's quite incremental in nature, in terms of both theoretical analysis and empirical results. Hence I vote for a weak reject.

content.title: Reply to review #2
content.comment:
Thank you for your valuable feedback and thoughtful reviews. Below we address your concerns about our work.

Q1. I am not very convinced by the claim that DP-LSSGD enjoys better utility guarantees under the same privacy budget. If we check the results in both convex and nonconvex cases in Table 1, it turns out the convergence rates (optimality/stationary gap) in terms of d, n and $\epsilon$ are the same between DP-SGD and DP-LSSGD. The only difference lies in the constants, which are fixed and do not matter much. If we check the results more carefully, it is even not clear in the convex case the constant $\gamma D_\sigma$ is smaller than $D_0$. From this perspective it is not clear to me what's the essential improvement here? 

A: Our utility bound for the convex optimization problem trades off the initialization (i.e., $D_\sigma$) and the Gaussian noise injection, and our numerical results show that the later one is the dominating term. Though the improvement of the utility bound is at a constant level, this constant is much less than one, especially for high dimensional problems. Also, our analysis is non-trivial.

Our major improvement lies in performance in real applications. Improving the performance of the DP machine learning (ML) models is one of the most important and challenging tasks in privacy-preserving ML. The proposed DP-LSSGD can significantly improve utility of the private models, especially in the high privacy regime (small $\epsilon$). For instance, within our testing regime, compared with the TensorFlow DP benchmark, DP-LSSGD can improve the accuracy of the DP logistic regression and DNN for MNIST classification by up to 3.78% and 5.0%, resp.

Moreover, the proposed DP-LSSGD is generally applicable to any setting that DP-SGD applies. We can use fast Fourier transform to compute the Laplacian smoothing (LS) with negligible overhead in memory and computational time. In the revision, we have made some detailed discussion on the theoretical utility bound and on the empirical benefit of DP-LSSGD in real applications.


Q2. The main idea of LS is to precondition the gradient descent by a fixed matrix $A_\sigma$. The authors claim that the LS method could help to avoid spurious minima and reduce the variance of SGD. I am not sure about this point, since in the literature there are many data-dependent preconditioning, including AdaGrad, Adam, AdaReg, etc., but none of them is free of the local-minima problem. So it's not clear to me why a fixed matrix will help here? The final DP-LSSGD algorithm is a combination of DPSGD with a preconditioning matrix given by $A_\sigma$, similar to what is done in LSSGD.
 
A: In the revised manuscript we have deleted the statement about avoiding spurious minima. Both avoiding spurious minima and reduce variance of SGD are the empirical results observed in [1]. In this paper, we leveraged the denoising property of the Laplacian matrix to improve the utility of the trained DP models.


Q3. The main contribution of this paper lies in Sec. 3, i.e., the theoretical analysis of the convergence rate of the proposed algorithm in both convex and nonconvex settings. The convergence rate are the same as the ones in the non-private settings. Just a comment, with further assumptions, e.g., strong convexity in the convex case, the authors could improve the $O(1/\epsilon)$ rate to linear convergence of $O(log(1/\epsilon))$. So the main take-home message here is that privacy does not sacrifice convergence speed, which is already known in the literature.

A: Yes, for the strongly convex problem, we can achieve a better convergence rate. In our paper, we focus on general convex and nonconvex problems.

We would like to emphasize that in practice, DP-LSSGD can remarkably improve utility of the trained DP models (Sec. 4), especially in the high privacy regime. Improving utility of the highly private ML models is challenging and of crucial importance in practice. The remarkable performance of DP-LSSGD is the most important contribution of our work.


Q4. Overall, I think there is indeed some novel contribution, but I feel it's incremental in nature, in terms of both theoretical analysis and empirical results. 

A: We appreciate your acknowledgment of paper's novel contribution. To the best of our knowledge, using LS to improve the utility of the DP model is a new idea and has never been studied before. The proposed algorithm is simple to use, and it can be applied to any settings where DP-SGD applies with negligible overhead. Numerically, we show the significant advantage of the DP-LSSGD compared with DP-SGD. We believe such a performance improvement is significant and should not be considered as incremental.

Our theoretical analysis includes both convergence under the DP optimization and the sharp bound for the Laplacian matrix as a denoising operator.

=========
We hope we have answered all your questions about our work, and we would appreciate more constructive feedback from you.
